land.text: Jintian in Guiping county, Guangxi, where the Jintian Uprising began in January 1851 (approximate position of Guiping)

predecessors.note: A rebel state born inside the Qing empire; it took no whole state's land at birth, only the Jintian base in Guangxi.

land.text: Nanjing (Tianjing) and the lower Yangtze land still held in 1864, retaken by Qing armies; Hong Tianguifu was captured on 25 October 1864 and the last Taiping army was wiped out in August 1871

successors.note: Cliopatria's last shape is 1864; the page dates the fall of Nanjing to 19 July 1864.

capitals.name: Tianjing (Nanjing)
capitals.note: Nanjing captured 19 March 1853 and renamed Tianjing; no capital is named for 1851-1852, when the army was on the march.

rulers.name: Hong Xiuquan (Heavenly King)
rulers.title: Heavenly King
rulers.note: Page table: August 1851 to May 1864; body text: died 1 June 1864 (food poisoning, suicide suggested). He declared himself Heavenly King on 11 January 1851.

rulers.name: Hong Tianguifu (Young Heavenly King)
rulers.title: Young Heavenly King
rulers.note: Page table: May to August 1864; captured by Qing forces on 25 October 1864.

correction.text: Jintian in Guiping county, Guangxi, where the Jintian Uprising began in January 1851 (approximate position of Guiping)

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria begins in 1853 but the page's infobox gives 'Jintian Uprising: 11 January 1851' as the founding. For 1851-1852 the movement was an army on the march (Hunan 1852, Wuchang December 1852) that held no territory the pages name beyond its Jintian base; a gap-filler may draw it as a small rebel zone.

224,376 km2 for 1853-55: Wuchang (Dec 1852), Anqing (Feb 1853) and Nanjing (19 March 1853) are the cities the page names; it gives no boundary. The infobox gives no area (only 'nearly 30 million people' at the peak), so the area check is by population: about 130 per km2 on the later 348,000 km2 peak, plausible for the lower Yangtze. The shape's western bbox edge (110.8 E, west of Wuchang) is not confirmed by the pages.

224,822 km2 for 1856 only: the shape is the 1853 shape plus a sliver; Wuchang was lost only in December 1856, so the year stands. The Tianjing Incident (Yang Xiuqing killed on Hong's orders) changed no border.

minus.text: Wuchang, retaken by Qing forces in December 1856

correction.text: the 1857 shape without Wuchang: 'Qing forces retook Wuchang in December 1856'

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria repeats the 1853 shape for 1857-1859, but the page dates the loss of Wuchang to December 1856, of Jiujiang to May 1858 and of the rest of Jiangxi to September 1858. This verdict is the 1857 shape without the Wuchang region; 1858-1859 are in the new keyframe taiping-heavenly-kingdom_1858.

union.text: Jiujiang and the rest of Jiangxi, taken by the Xiang Army in May-September 1858

correction.text: the 1857 shape without Wuchang and Jiangxi

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for 1858-1859: Wuchang gone (December 1856), then 'The Xiang Army captured Jiujiang in May 1858 and the rest of Jiangxi by September'. What is left on the pages is Nanjing, Anqing and the Anhui-Jiangsu land between them.

283,395 km2: Hangzhou (19 March 1860), Changzhou (26 May) and Suzhou (2 June) taken after the break of the siege of Nanjing; the bbox now reaches 120.9 E, as Suzhou (120.6 E) and Hangzhou (120.2 E) require. The Shanghai attempt (A: August 1860; B: June 1861 to 1862) failed, so Shanghai is outside the shape.

347,846 km2, the peak: Ningbo taken 9 December and Hangzhou (again) 31 December 1861; Anqing was lost to the Xiang Army in 1861. The pages do not say which land the Taiping held in Jiangxi and Hubei in 1861, so the shape's western reach (113.5 E) is unverified: page budget.

231,470 km2 for 1862-63: Ningbo retaken 10 May 1862 with the Ever Victorious Army (D: formed 1860, named by the Qing in March 1862); Xiang Army besieges Nanjing from May 1862; Shanghai repulsed. The shape no longer reaches Ningbo or the west of Anhui, as the pages require.

185,942 km2, the last year: Nanjing's investment completed 2 March 1864 and the city fell 19 July 1864; D: 'By early 1864, Qing control in most areas was reestablished'. The dates of the fall of Suzhou, Changzhou and Hangzhou are not on the pages opened.

region.text: Jintian in Guiping county, Guangxi, where the Jintian Uprising began in January 1851 (approximate position of Guiping)

ledger.note: 1851: Hong Xiuquan proclaims the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom at Jintian in Guangxi. The infobox gives 'Jintian Uprising: 11 January 1851'; Hong declared himself 'Heavenly King' on that date and the rebels 'routed Qing forces stationed in Jintian' (Taiping Rebellion page).

1852: the Taiping army marches north through Hunan and takes Wuchang on the Yangtze. 'They captured Wuchang in December 1852 after reaching the Yangtze River'; they had besieged Changsha and occupied Yuezhou first (no dates for those).
1853: Anqing falls to the Taiping in February. 'The Taiping captured Anqing in February 1853.'

region.text: Nanjing, captured on 19 March 1853 and renamed Tianjing, the Taiping capital to 19 July 1864

ledger.note: 1853: the Taiping take Nanjing and make it their capital, Tianjing. 'On March 19, 1853, the Taipings captured the city of Nanjing' and renamed it Tianjing (infobox 'Capture of Nanjing: 19 March 1853').
1853: the capital is Tianjing (Nanjing). 'In 1853, the Taiping forces captured Nanjing, making it their capital and renaming it Tianjing.'

region.text: Wuchang, retaken by Qing forces in December 1856

ledger.note: 1856: Qing forces retake Wuchang. 'Qing forces retook Wuchang in December 1856.' The Tianjing Incident of the same year (Yang Xiuqing killed on Hong's orders) moved no border.

region.text: Jiujiang, captured by the Xiang Army in May 1858

ledger.note: 1858: the Xiang Army takes Jiujiang. 'The Xiang Army captured Jiujiang in May 1858.'

region.text: the rest of Jiangxi, taken by the Xiang Army by September 1858

ledger.note: 1858: the rest of Jiangxi falls to the Xiang Army by September. 'and the rest of Jiangxi by September' (the page does not list the places, so the whole province is my reading).

region.text: southern Jiangsu and northern Zhejiang: Hangzhou, Changzhou and Suzhou

ledger.note: 1860: the Taiping break the siege of Nanjing and take Hangzhou on 19 March, Changzhou on 26 May and Suzhou on 2 June. Taking Hangzhou and Suzhou 'to the east' is also in the infobox article.

region.text: Shanghai and its treaty-port approaches, the target of the Taiping attacks of 1860-1862

ledger.note: 1860: the Taiping attack Shanghai. 'An attempt to take Shanghai in August 1860 was initially successful but finally repulsed' by Chinese and European forces (the Taiping Rebellion page dates the attempt to June 1861 and says it was repulsed after 15 months; January 1862 the Taiping surround the city).

region.text: Anqing, captured by the Xiang Army in 1861

ledger.note: 1861: the Xiang Army captures Anqing with a Royal Navy blockade, around the death of the Xianfeng Emperor. The page gives the year, not the month.
1861: the Eastern Expedition takes Ningbo on 9 December and Hangzhou on 31 December. 'Ningbo was captured on December 9, and Hangzhou was besieged and captured on December 31.'
1862: the attack on Shanghai is beaten. The Ever Victorious Army 'repulsed another attack on Shanghai in 1862'; B: 'In January 1862, Taiping troops surrounded Shanghai but could not take it.'
1862: Ningbo is retaken on 10 May with the help of the Ever Victorious Army. Described as 'helped retake Ningbo on May 10'.

region.text: Nanjing, captured on 19 March 1853 and renamed Tianjing, the Taiping capital to 19 July 1864

ledger.note: 1862: the Xiang Army besieges Tianjing. 'In May 1862, the Xiang Army besieged Nanjing' (the investment was completed only on 2 March 1864, Third Battle of Nanking page).

region.text: the Taiping cities of southern Jiangsu and Zhejiang outside Nanjing

ledger.note: 1864: Qing armies reconquer the Taiping land in Jiangsu and Zhejiang outside Nanjing (Suzhou, Changzhou, Hangzhou). The pages opened are silent on the dates: D says only 'By early 1864, Qing control in most areas was reestablished' and the Ever Victorious Army was disbanded in May 1864; the Li Xiucheng page says the Huai Army's victories led 'to the surrender of Suzhou' after July 1863. The year is bridged from Cliopatria's 1864 shape.

region.text: Nanjing, captured on 19 March 1853 and renamed Tianjing, the Taiping capital to 19 July 1864

ledger.note: 1864: Tianjing falls. The siege (14 March to 19 July 1864) ended when 'the attackers detonated the explosives in the tunnel under Taiping Gate' and 'by the evening every gate of the city was firmly in the hands of Qing forces'.

region.text: the 1864 remnant of the Heavenly Kingdom: Tianjing and the land around it, retaken by the Qing

ledger.note: 1864: Nanjing falls on 19 July and the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom ends. Hong Xiuquan had died on 1 June; Li Xiucheng was captured on 22 July and executed on 7 August; Lai Wenguang broke out with 3,000 horse and joined the Nien; Hong Tianguifu was taken on 25 October 1864 (infobox of the main article) and the last army was destroyed in August 1871.

wars.name: Taiping Rebellion

zones.text: the lower Yangtze: Nanjing, Suzhou, Hangzhou, Ningbo and the approaches of Shanghai

wars.outcome: Qing victory: Nanjing fell on 19 July 1864 and the Heavenly Kingdom ended; remnants were hunted down until January 1866 and a last army was destroyed in August 1871.
wars.note: The page gives the Taiping a population of 'nearly 30 million' at the peak; it does not list the provinces held.

wars.name: Taiping Northern Expedition
wars.outcome: Failure: 'The attempt to take Beijing failed'; 'The Northern expedition was a complete failure'. The pages give no dates or northern limit, and no ground was held.
wars.note: Zones left empty: the expedition held no land the pages name.

wars.name: Taiping Western Expedition

zones.text: Jiangxi, where Jiujiang fell to the Xiang Army in May 1858

wars.outcome: Limited success: 'the Western achieved limited success'; the Taiping held Wuchang until December 1856 and Jiangxi until 1858. The page names no cities for the expedition.

wars.name: Battle of Shanghai (1860-1862)

zones.text: Shanghai and the thirty-mile circle in which the Ever Victorious Army operated

wars.outcome: Repulsed: Chinese and European forces defeated the Taiping attempts on Shanghai; the Ever Victorious Army, named by the Qing in March 1862, 'repulsed another attack on Shanghai in 1862'.
wars.note: A dates the first attempt to August 1860; B to June 1861 with Shanghai surrounded in January 1862; D gives 1862 for the last repulse.

wars.name: Third Battle of Nanking
wars.outcome: Qing victory: investment completed 2 March 1864; the city fell on 19 July 1864 and burned until 26 July; Li Xiucheng was captured on 22 July; over 200,000 Taiping troops surrendered.
wars.note: The Xiang Army besieged Nanjing from May 1862; the battle's own dates are 14 March to 19 July 1864.

certainty.note: A rebel state with moving fronts: the Taiping held cities and the roads between them, and the pages give no boundary lines. The Yangtze cities (Nanjing, Anqing, Suzhou, Hangzhou, Ningbo) are firm points; everything between is approximate.

notes: Page budget (5) spent on the main article, the Taiping Rebellion, the Third Battle of Nanking, the Ever Victorious Army and Li Xiucheng. Not on the pages: the dates of the Qing reconquest of Suzhou (Dec 1863), Changzhou, Hangzhou (1864), Huzhou and the Zhejiang cities; the western limits of the Taiping holdings in Hubei, Jiangxi and Anhui in 1861; the extent of the Northern Expedition. These are confidence 1 or left to a gap-filler (pages that would help: Battle of Suzhou, Zuo Zongtang, Li Hongzhang, Zeng Guofan). The Taiping Rebellion page lists no area; Cliopatria's 348,000 km2 peak is checked only against 'nearly 30 million' people. Cliopatria starts in 1853; the dossier starts in January 1851 (Jintian Uprising) and adds a 1851-1852 keyframe for the army on the march. Cliopatria repeats one shape for 1857-1859 although Wuchang (1856) and Jiangxi (1858) were lost: fixed with the new keyframe taiping-heavenly-kingdom_1858. Shi Dakai's army (surrendered near Chengdu in 1863) and the remnants after 1864 (Wang Haiyang beaten on 29 January 1866; Li Fuzhong's army wiped out in August 1871) held no mapped land. Gazetteer: no place entry for Jintian or Guiping (a coordinate is used). The qing-dynasty counterpart is written by ea-08-b; the Nien rebels (Lai Wenguang joined them) have no dossier here.
